title: Holiday shipping tips for small sellers
excerpt: Carrier cut-off dates, label stock planning and five habits that keep peak-season orders moving.
body: Peak season can double or triple your daily order count. The sellers who stay calm in December are the ones who plan their supplies in October.
## Stock labels before you need them
Count how many labels you used last November and December, then add 30%. Fanfold stacks of 2,000 mean fewer reloads on busy days, and tier pricing means the extra stock costs less per label.
## Know the carrier cut-offs
USPS, UPS and FedEx publish holiday shipping deadlines every year. Put them on your calendar and on your store banner so customers order in time.
## Batch your printing
Print labels in batches instead of one by one. Integrated labels with paper receipts let you print the packing slip and label in one pass.
## Keep a spare printer path
If your thermal printer goes down, laser half-sheet labels keep orders moving from any office printer.

title: Direct thermal vs thermal transfer: which label do you need?
excerpt: Ribbon or no ribbon? How long the print lasts, which printers you need and what each material is best for.
body: Both materials print with heat, but they work very differently - and choosing the right one saves money and headaches.
## Direct thermal

Direct thermal labels have a heat-sensitive coating that darkens where the print head touches it. No ribbon, no ink. They are ideal for shipping labels that only need to last a few weeks to a few months.
## Thermal transfer
Thermal transfer printers melt ink from a ribbon onto the label. The image lasts for years and resists heat, sunlight and abrasion - the right choice for inventory, asset tags and product barcodes.
## Quick rule of thumb
If it ships, choose direct thermal. If it stays on a shelf, a pallet or a product for months, choose thermal transfer.

title: How to load fanfold labels in your thermal printer
excerpt: A two-minute setup for Rollo, Zebra and other desktop printers - plus how to avoid jams and skipped labels.
body: Fanfold labels feed from a stack behind or under the printer, so there is no spindle to fight with.
## 1. Place the stack
Set the stack behind the printer with the label side facing up and the first label pointing toward the feed slot.
## 2. Feed the first label
Open the printer, pull the first label through the rear slot and guide it under the sensor. Adjust the guides so they touch the liner edges without squeezing.
## 3. Calibrate
Close the printer and run the auto-calibration (on most Rollo and Zebra models, hold the feed button). The printer will find the gap between labels.
## Avoiding jams
Keep the stack square and directly behind the slot, and do not let the folded stack lean against a wall.
